properties.decision:
Anthony, 2026-08-26, from the same brainstorm: *"what would make the agent say, I have the perfect skill or tool needed for problem X?"*

**RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.**

═══ THE MISMATCH, STATED PRECISELY ═══

An agent holds a PROBLEM in the user's words. reflow2 offers ~150 tools named for the OPERATION they perform. Retrieval has to cross that gap, and `find_tools` crosses it by matching text against tool names and descriptions — which works when the user already speaks reflow2 and fails exactly when they do not.

**Two measurements, both from asking a user's question in a user's words:**

- *"does my declared decomposition match the real coupling?"* — best of 152 tools was **`set_interface_designation`**, and the session's actual finding came from a hand-written Python script.
- *"move a component to a different parent"* — returned **`contain_component`**, which ADDS a parent and never removes the old one. The discoverable sequence CAUSES the `multiple_parents` defect.

The second is worse than a miss: retrieval succeeded, was confidently wrong, and produced a defect. **A ranked list with no notion of "this is not what you want" is not a weak answer, it is a misleading one.**

And `dec:bl-155` names the same disease from the other end — its group (c), the *"uncomfortable middle"*: `evidence_report`, `seam_report`, `budget_report`, `dimension_drift`, `analyze_alternatives`, `arrival_delta` are READS that answer real questions on designs that exist today, and nobody reaches for them. Its own words: *"a capability nobody can find is worth what an absent one is worth."*

═══ OPTIONS, none chosen ═══

**(a) A question-shaped index, HARVESTED rather than authored.** Map "questions a user actually asks" → tool. The corpus already exists: `tools/surface_usage.py` read 46 transcripts and 6,095 calls. Mine the prose that PRECEDED each call and you get real question→tool pairs, in users' words, for free. ⚠️ Counter: it learns what agents already do, so it can only reinforce the tools already being found — the 40 never-called tools have no preceding prose to mine. It would sharpen the head of the distribution and do nothing for the tail, which is the part that hurts.

**(b) Question-shaped ALIASES over the existing names.** `"what will this break?"` → `propagate_change`; `"has this been decided?"` → `search_design`; `"what did I just make false?"` → `unclaimed_findings`. Additive, no consumer breakage, and it puts the user's register on the surface where `find_tools` can match it. ⚠️ Counter: a second naming system to keep in step with the first, and nothing detects an alias that has gone stale.

**(c) Rename the tools after the question they answer.** The honest version of (b), and the one `fix-properly-not-patch` argues for before 1.0. ⚠️ Counter: ~150 renames, every consumer breaks, and it trades a retrieval problem for a migration problem. Also the operation name is the RIGHT name for the agent that already knows what it wants.

**(d) One door: a dispatcher that takes free-text intent and returns the skill, the tools AND the traps.** *"I am about to X"* → everything relevant, including what will go wrong. ⚠️ Counter: an agent that would not call `list_skills` has no more reason to call the door. Adds a layer to a surface already accused of being large.

**(e) Make the tool say when it is the WRONG answer.** The `contain_component` case argues this is worth more than better ranking: a tool that knows the adjacent mistake can name it in its own description. Some already do. ⚠️ Counter: it improves precision after retrieval, not retrieval itself — no help for a tool never surfaced at all.

═══ THE OBSERVATION UNDERNEATH ═══

Retrieval is a fourth leg beside the three already recorded (**typed tool + instruction + detector that notices absence**). Those three make a vocabulary REACHABLE. None makes it RETRIEVABLE from a problem in someone else's words — and reachable-but-not-retrievable is exactly what BL-155's group (c) measures.
properties.name: OPEN — what would let a problem stated in the USER'S words retrieve the tool that answers it, when the tool is named for the operation it performs?
properties.rationale:
Kept separate from the four-layer diagnostic because it is a different question with a different answer shape: that one asks WHERE use fails, this one asks HOW a problem finds its tool. Retrieval sits mostly in layer ① (known) with a foot in ② (recognised), and could be built and tested without settling which layer is the bottleneck.

The two failed retrievals are recorded with the tool each returned, rather than as "find_tools is weak", because the second one — a confidently wrong answer that causes a defect — argues for a different fix than the first, and collapsing them would lose that.
